mcqs.question: Why does MonotonicIdGenerator use an atomic long with an increment-and-get operation instead of a plain field with a bare increment?
options: Because plain numeric fields cannot be declared final
Because increment-and-get is faster to read in code, with no effect on correctness
Because a plain field would require allocating a new object on every call
A bare increment is a read-modify-write sequence, not atomic, so concurrent threads could read the same value before either writes back and produce a duplicate ID
mcqs.explanation: Only an atomic operation prevents two threads from both reading the same pre-increment value under concurrency, which a bare increment cannot guarantee. Final-ness of fields, allocation behavior, and readability are all unrelated to the actual correctness problem being solved here.

mcqs.question: Which ID scheme is the right default when multiple independent processes must generate IDs with zero coordination and ordering doesn't matter?
options: A composite of timestamp plus a per-process counter
A sequential database auto-increment column shared by all processes
mcqs.explanation: A UUID needs no coordination between processes and doesn't require ordering, matching exactly what's asked. A single shared counter or a shared database sequence both require coordination across processes, and the composite is the right pick only when some rough ordering is actually needed.

mcqs.question: Why does it matter whether a generated ID will be exposed to end users?
options: User-facing IDs must always be shorter than internal IDs
A sequential ID exposed publicly leaks information, like approximate volume, and lets users guess and probe for adjacent records
End users cannot process IDs longer than a few characters
It has no real effect — any ID scheme is equally safe to expose
mcqs.explanation: A predictable sequential ID reveals volume trends and enables ID-guessing attacks against adjacent records once it's public, which is the actual risk. There's no length restriction users can't handle, and the exposure risk very much depends on the scheme chosen.

mcqs.question: Why is generating an ID from a naive random number generator, with no analysis of the ID space, risky at scale?
options: Random number generators cannot produce values large enough to be useful as IDs
It requires more CPU than an atomic counter, making it too slow for production use
The collision probability grows faster than intuition suggests as more IDs are generated, especially with a small ID space or weak randomness source
It's actually a safe and standard approach with no real downside
mcqs.explanation: The birthday-paradox effect means collision probability rises faster than most people expect as the count of generated IDs grows, particularly with a limited ID space. Random generators can absolutely produce large values, raw CPU cost isn't the core issue, and this is a real, common mistake rather than a safe default.
